messages.body_plain:
The rw2d model is a more direct translation of the pspline2dimrw1 model, except it uses 2nd order difference penalties instead of first order differences:
  http://www.math.ntnu.no/inla/r-inla.org/doc/latent/rw2d-model.pdf

The spde alternative can be used in a way that allows 2nd order b-spline bases for a squared second order derivatives penalty model, but currently you'd need to use inla.mesh.1d() and inla.mesh.1d.fem() and kronecker() to construct a precision matrix to feed into a "generic0" model, as we don't have a wrapper function for this kind of model.
The "read this first" tutorial has a 1d example of a penalized spline model with 2nd order basis functions.

Finn

At the moment, I'm doing some exploratory INLA fitting with SPDE on each outcome univariately, but I'd like to fit the models jointly. If the correlation between Y1 and Y2 was constant in space, I'd use the Kronecker product model tools implemented in INLA with exponential correlation and set my grouping to consist of my two outcomes.

Is there any way to extend the Kronecker product model to allow for a spatially varying correlation? Possibly something that allows me to use the SPDE tools to build up a finite element approximation to the correlation structure?

much thanks,
Aaron

On Thu, 2015-04-16 at 09:42 -0700, Víctor Hugo Gutiérrez Vélez wrote:

>
> Would you explain me why rescaling a covariate (x) is giving me
> comparable modeling outputs when I assume a linear effect on the
> response (y) but NOT when I assume a nonlinear effect?

Hi,

this is because the prior is kept fixed, hence rescaling x implicitely
change the prior.

You'll see his effect also in the fixed-effects, looking at the stdev

> inla(y~x, data=data.frame(y=0,x=1))$summary.fixed["x","sd"]
[1] 31.62277669
> inla(y~x, data=data.frame(y=0,x=1111111))$summary.fixed["x","sd"]
[1] 0.2453530524

so you need to adjust control.fixed=list(prec=...)  so that the
'effective' prior is the same.

Using 'rw2', the issue is the same, but there is more to it.

	f(x, model="rw2")

and

	xx = x * 1000
	f(xx, model="rw2")

would behave VERY different. It is the same issue as above, additional
to the behaviour of RW2 which also depends on the length(x). This is
discussed in detail in this tutorial,

http://www.r-inla.org/examples/tutorials/tutorial-on-option-scale-model

arguing for that its best to use

	f(xx, model="rw2", scale=TRUE)

which will rescale the model so that using 'x' and 'xx' is the same.

Best
H

I think the problem is that the data aren't informative enough. You
only have slightly more than 2 observations per location, so you don't
have a lot of data to estimate any of the levels of the random effect
(each observation can only be 0 or 1, so you have a small number of
possible values available). The hyper-parameter is thus also poorly
estimated. You thus either need more structure on the location level
(a spatial model? location-level covariates? Group location into
region?), or you should remove it because it's never going to be
informative.

Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

Thanks for your reply, the idea of using random effect is to account for over-dispersion and independence issue in the data, because we suspect that samples from the same location are not entirely independent from each other. Hence model assumptions under standard logistic would be violated.

You are right in that there are large number of levels in the random effect which only contain 1 or 2 observations, but some levels having as many as 40 observations. If i have a list of other location-level variables (such as location type, size of farm etc), will this improve the estimation? Bare in mind that each sample from the same location would have the same location-level variable also.

Grouping into regions may increase the size in each random effect, but the independence issue would still be unresolved right?

Thanks again for your time and help on this.

Cheers

Siben

messages.body_plain:
On 17 Apr 2015, at 20:13, KTM <morrison...@gmail.com> wrote:

> The glmmAK package for current version of R is archived and I'd like to play around with GMRF as I work my way through the Rue & Held text, but would rather not have to use the C library directly if possible. Is it possible to interact with the library through the INLA package now instead? Or any other packages currently available?

Yes, there is partial access to the GMRFLib methods vie the inla package interface.
Off the top of my head, here's a (partial) list of the relevant functions (see the help texts for more info).
inla.qsolve
inla.qreordering
inla.qreorderings
inla.qinv
inla.qsample

There is no direct support for access to the Cholesky factors, but you can combine your own calls to inla.qreordering and Matrix::chol, Matrix::Cholesky, or spam::chol (and then regular solve) to compute things using the more low-level techniques, you also need that to compute log-determinants.

inla.qinv calculates the elements of the inverse of Q for which Q_{ij} is nonzero, plus some additional elements.  This gives access to marginal variances and covariances between neighbours.

Q needs to be a sparseMatrix object.

Finn L

messages.subject: inla.posterior.sample inaccuracy?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I'm trying to validate the samples generated with inla.posterior.sample. A simple independent Gaussian simulation gives me unbiased estimates as validated with 95% CI. However, a little bit more complicated Poisson AR(1) time-series example gives me underestimates. Could it be inaccuracy in INLA or perhaps a mistake in my code? Here is the parallelized code, where I first sample from AR(1) which gives expectation vector lambda to randomize from Poisson distribution, I fit the time-series with INLA Poisson AR(1) and check if the lambda vector falls within 95% and 50% CIs (should give around 95% and 50% but I got 81% and 41%):

library(INLA)
library(parallel)
library(doMC)
registerDoMC(cores=detectCores())
library(plyr)

n.t <- 20
n.posterior.samples <- 1000
n.iterations <- 1000

p <- ldply(1:n.iterations, function(i) {
  message("Iteration ", i)

  lambda <- exp(1 + arima.sim(model=list(ar=c(.7)), n=n.t))
  y <- rpois(n.t, lambda)
  data <- data.frame(y=y, t=1:n.t)

  result <- try(inla(y ~ 1 + f(t, model="ar1"), data=data, family="poisson", control.compute=list(config=TRUE)))
  if (inherits(result, "try-error")) return(NULL)
  samples <- inla.posterior.sample(n.posterior.samples, result)
  predictor <- exp(sapply(samples, function(x) x$latent[1:n.t,]))

  p95 <- 0
  p50 <- 0
  for (j in 1:n.t) {
    ci <- quantile(predictor[j,], c(.025, .975))
    p95 <- p95 + (ci[1] <= lambda[j] & ci[2] >= lambda[j])
    ci <- quantile(predictor[j,], c(.25, .75))
    p50 <- p50 + (ci[1] <= lambda[j] & ci[2] >= lambda[j])
  }

  return(data.frame(p95=p95, p50=p50))
}, .parallel=T)

mean(p$p95) / n.t # =0.81135
mean(p$p50) / n.t # =0.405

On 20 April 2015 at 22:56,  <azi...@uw.edu> wrote:
> My data is distributed randomly in space and to get my 'fitted values' I add in a datastack at the same locations as
> my original data but with NAs listed as the outcome.

The result of that should be (nearly) identical to the fitted values
given for the actual data values, since it's just the linear
predictor.  See below for what you more realistically can use.

> my data locations. My question is, is there any fast or easy way to
> interpolate and plot these residual estimates (which are not on the SPDE
> mesh or on any grid) onto a regular grid over spatial my domain with the
> built-in INLA functions?

Since the residuals are defined only for the data locations, and are
essentially independent (in the perfect model case) it doesn't make
sense to interpolate them.  For plotting residuals,
fields::quilt.plot() is a good option.

The field itself can however easily be interpolated onto a grid; see
inla.mesh.project() and inla.mesh.projector() (or more low-level by
directly multiplying with a matrix constructed with
inla.spde.make.A()).

Depending what you're going to do with the residuals, you may want to
consider leave-one-out crossvalidated residuals instead of the raw
residuals.  These can, for Gaussian observation errors, be obtained
approximately by a
simple postprocessing (exact calculations are more tricky, and may
involve sampling from the posterior).  See Section
2.3 of
  http://people.bath.ac.uk/fl353/tmp/gmrf.pdf
for the needed calculation, where y_i - E_{(i)} are the
cross-validated residuals.
Also note that inla() can calculate a type of cross-validated residual
that also handles the non-Gaussian observation case; see
?control.inla, option "cpo".

> Maybe something that automatically performs Kriging
> to a grid using the fitted INLA model? Pointers to a function or a tutorial
> that I've missed would be greatly appreciated.

This would make sense in the case that the model did _not_ fully model
the data, so that there is "leftover correlation".  But then that
leftover correlation would need to be modelled, so the "correct"
solution in the Bayesian setting would be to run a new model on the
original data, with a new model component capable of handling the
leftover correlation.  In a stepwise residual modelling approach, one
would just take the residuals and estimate that extra model component
directly using only the residuals, which could be done with another
inla() model.

Finn

No, only the copy has the extra parameter. Think of the case where you have more than one extra copy; then the reciprocal construction you describe wouldn't be possible.

It is however possible to symmetries this by precisely doing that; make _two_ copies, and have all NA in the original f().
f(dummy, ...) + f(i1, copy="dummy", fixed=FALSE) + f(i2, copy="dummy",fixed=FALSE)
Where dummy=rep(NA, n) and you need to specify some more parameters to that f() to tell inla how big the model should be etc.
In this case the "dummy" model has an unidentifiable scaling parameter, so you would want to fixed that parameter to avoid overparameterisation.
(I know of one person who have used this approach successfully.)

messages.subject_clean: Running INLA from within the server problems
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm running some long and memory consuming models, which run fine. I use a linux server, and I use inla(...,inla.call = 'submit',...) or (...,inla.call = 'remote',...)
and they use multiple cores. However, in need of speed, I have access to other linux servers where I would like to run some other models.

So, first, is there a way to configure more than one server for the inla remote/submit call?

Since I didn't find this, I went ahead and just ran INLA within the server (opened R from within the server and ran INLA). However, it seems that inla is not properly
taking advantage of all the cores/RAM in the server. Looking at 'top', there is no "inla64" running, just R using a single core. Because of the memory
requirements, it crashes early on with:

Error: C stack usage  10188999 is too close to the limit

Any ideas on how to solve this?

R version in server:
 R version 3.1.2 (2014-10-31)

Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit)

INLA version on server:

INLA_0.0-1420281647

Any help would be much appreciated,

Ignacio

On Thu, 2015-04-30 at 08:11 -0700, ignacio quintero wrote:

>
> So, first, is there a way to configure more than one server for the
> inla remote/submit call?

Hi,

I have been waiting years for this question... By now, only one remote
host is defined, and I do not know (have not decided) how to extend it.
If someone has suggestions, please let me know.

one option is to extend the call as

	inla(..., inla.call = "remote@host")

which will use ~/.inlarc-host, and simular with 'submit' and those. this
gives a lot of files, maybe better to let remote@host  define a
variable, like INLAHOST and peple can then make the ~/.inlarc file
depend on it, like

	case $INLAHOST in ...
	esac

which would require shell-scripting knowledge (in (ba)sh shell).

well, until we decide, you can always use this workaround...

	Sys.setenv(INLAHOST="hostname")
	r = inla(..., inla.call = "remote")

and then the variable INLAHOST is defined when ~/.inlarc in sourced, so
you can switch of 'if' there, to chost host.

> Since I didn't find this, I went ahead and just ran INLA within the
> server (opened R from within the server and ran INLA). However, it
> seems that inla is not properly
> taking advantage of all the cores/RAM in the server. Looking at 'top',
> there is no "inla64" running, just R using a single core.

seems like it hasn't come the inla64-part yet.

> Because of the memory
> requirements, it crashes early on with:
>
> Error: C stack usage  10188999 is too close to the limit

maybe you need

	ulimit -s unlimited

in your .bashrc or something, to set the stack-limit to 'unlimited'.
Maybe this the issue?

H
